opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it gets at something pretty fundamental about how these model families differ.

The way I like to think about it is that attention, in its standard form, doesn't really compress history at all. It keeps a cache of everything it's seen, every token's keys and values, and then at each step it can go back and look at any of it directly. That's what makes it so powerful for things like exact recall or copying, but it's also why the cost grows with the sequence length.

Most efficient attention variants, whether that's sparse attention, sliding windows, or low-rank and kernel approximations, are still fundamentally operating within that paradigm. They're asking, "How do we approximate that full lookup more cheaply?" So they might drop some tokens, restrict which tokens can attend to which, or approximate the attention matrix. But the underlying mental model is still a cache you query into, and the compression is kind of a lossy shortcut on top of that.

State space models start from a different place. They're recurrent at their core. You have a fixed-size state, and as each new input comes in, you update that state. The state *is* the compressed summary of the entire history. There's no going back to look at raw tokens; everything the model knows about the past has to live in that state. So the question becomes, "What's the best way to update this state so it keeps what matters?"

That's where a lot of our work has focused. Early on with things like HiPPO and S4, it was about principled ways of making the state represent a long history, like projecting onto polynomial bases so you have a mathematically grounded memory. Then with Mamba, the key idea was selectivity: making the state updates depend on the input, so the model can decide what to remember, what to ignore, and when to reset. That's a big part of what made SSMs competitive on language, because language needs content-dependent filtering.

So I'd say the distinction is something like: efficient attention approximates a lossless memory, while SSMs learn a lossy memory directly. Each has tradeoffs. SSMs are very efficient, constant memory at inference, and they handle long contexts gracefully, but because they compress, they can struggle with tasks needing precise retrieval of an arbitrary earlier detail. Attention is great at that but expensive.

And honestly, that's why I think hybrids are so interesting. Once you see these as two different kinds of memory, a compressed state versus a retrievable cache, it's natural to combine them. A lot of what we've seen is that a mostly-SSM model with a few attention layers gets you most of the efficiency and most of the recall. With work like Mamba-2 and structured state space duality, we've also shown these families are mathematically closer than they look; certain forms of linear attention and SSMs are two views of the same computation. So the boundary is blurrier than people think, but the intuition of "compress versus cache" is still a useful way to think about it.

r001.rationale: The response says an SSM keeps a fixed-size state that summarizes the entire history, with no access to raw past tokens.

r002.rationale: It identifies sparse attention and other efficient variants as dropping tokens or restricting attention, framing these as ways to make lookup cheaper.

r003.rationale: The response separately describes efficient attention dropping tokens and SSMs deciding what to remember, but does not connect adaptive attention’s history selection to the SSM goal of compressing history into an informative state.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is that it comes down to what you're actually optimizing when you compress. A state space model, or really any recurrent model, is forced to maintain a fixed-size state. Every token that comes in has to get folded into that state, and then it's gone. So the model is doing lossy compression by construction. There's no option to go back and look at the raw history. And the interesting question becomes: how do you decide what to keep? Mamba's selection mechanism is basically our answer to that. It's letting the model, based on the current input, decide how much to update the state and how much to forget, so the compression becomes content-dependent instead of a fixed filter.

Efficient attention mechanisms are coming from the opposite direction. Standard attention doesn't compress at all. The KV cache grows linearly, and every query can look at every past token exactly. That's its superpower and its cost. So most of the efficient attention work, whether that's linear attention, sparse patterns, low-rank approximations, is starting from this lossless object and asking how to make it cheaper. Some of those end up being recurrent in disguise. Linear attention, if you unroll it, is literally a recurrence with a matrix-valued state, which is why there's been all this convergence between the two families lately. But the design philosophy is different. They're approximating attention, and the question is how much accuracy you lose relative to the full thing. We're starting from the state and asking how expressive we can make it.

And I think that difference in framing actually matters for where the models are good and bad. If your task is something like needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, where you genuinely need exact recall of one arbitrary token, attention is the right inductive bias and any compressed state is going to struggle at some length. But a lot of what language modeling is doing isn't that. It's building up a more abstract summary of the context, and a well-designed state that's been trained to select what matters can be a lot more efficient, both in compute and sometimes in generalization. So I don't think of it as one being strictly better. I think of them as two different notions of memory, and the hybrid architectures people are building now are kind of the admission that you probably want both.

r001.rationale: It says each token is folded into a fixed-size state and then is gone, describing lossy compression, and characterizes language modeling as building an abstract summary of context.

r002.rationale: It lists sparse patterns and other efficient attention methods, but does not identify choosing which past tokens to retain in a history cache as their efficiency mechanism.

r003.rationale: It describes Mamba’s input-dependent state updates, but does not connect adaptive attention’s selection of remembered history to the SSM compression objective.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful way to distinguish them is to ask what gets kept as the sequence gets longer. In standard attention, you keep a representation of every token, and then a future query can look back at those representations. Efficient attention covers a lot of approaches, but some of them compress that collection of keys and values so that you don’t have to store or access the entire history.

A state space model starts with a different formulation: you have a fixed-size state, and each new input updates that state. So everything you know about the past has to pass through that update. The model has to learn what information to preserve and what information to discard, before it knows exactly what a future input might ask for.

But the distinction isn’t absolute. Linear attention, for example, can also be written as a recurrent update with a fixed-size state. So it’s less that one compresses history and the other doesn’t, and more about the structure of the compression: what update rule you use, how information persists, and how you read it back out.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts per-token representations in attention with an SSM’s fixed-size state, through which information about the past must pass.

r002.rationale: It says some efficient attention methods compress keys and values, but does not identify choosing which past tokens to retain in a history cache.

r003.rationale: It says SSMs learn what information to preserve or discard, but does not connect that objective to adaptive attention selecting which history to remember.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is what you keep in that compressed state. With something like linear attention, you’re typically taking the keys and values and accumulating them into a fixed-size summary. Then a query comes along and reads from that summary. So you’re preserving this key-value retrieval interpretation of attention, but approximating it in a way that doesn’t require storing the whole history.

A state space model starts from a different perspective: you have a state that evolves over time. Every new input updates that state, and the dynamics determine which information is retained, how it changes, and how quickly it decays. So the compression is really a learned dynamical process.

There’s actually a lot of overlap mathematically. You can write linear attention as a particular kind of recurrent state update. So I wouldn’t draw a hard boundary between them. The useful question is what structure you put into that update, and whether it gives the model the ability to remember and retrieve the information the task needs.

r001.rationale: The response describes an evolving state and learned compression, but does not clearly say that the state abstracts history without preserving individual past-token identities.

r002.rationale: It describes linear attention accumulating keys and values into a fixed-size summary, but does not identify selecting past tokens for a history cache as an efficiency mechanism.

r003.rationale: It discusses information retained by SSM dynamics and key-value retrieval in linear attention, but does not connect adaptive attention’s selection of history to the SSM goal of producing a smaller informative state.
